stem: A 14-year-old, previously healthy girl is brought to the office due to recurrent headaches.  The patient has had 4 episodes of severe, throbbing pain on the right side of her head over the last 2 months, with the most recent occurring a week ago.  The headaches are often associated with nausea, and the patient has had occasional vomiting.  Lying in a dark room after taking acetaminophen improves the pain.  The episodes resolve after 4-5 hours.  The patient has had no visual disturbances or focal weakness but has experienced tingling and numbness affecting the right upper extremity prior to onset of the headaches.  Vital signs are within normal limits.  Physical examination, including funduscopic and neurologic evaluation, shows no abnormalities.  Which of the following is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's current condition?​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌

options.label: C
options.text: Hypothalamic orexin A and B peptides

explanation:
This patient with a normal neurologic examination has episodic, throbbing, unilateral headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and light sensitivity, findings characteristic of migraines.  An aura may precede the headache in some patients and is most commonly visual (eg, scotoma) or sensory (eg, unilateral extremity paresthesia).

The pathogenesis of migraines is multifactorial, and is thought to involve a genetic predisposition to increased cerebral excitability, allowing a wave of cortical depolarization with subsequent suppression (cortical spreading depression) that propagates across the cerebral cortex; this abnormal activity is likely involved in generating the pre-headache aura.

Cortical spreading depression causes extracellular ion shifts and release of inflammatory mediators that sensitize and activate trigeminal nociceptors extending throughout the meninges and intracranial vasculature, causing pain in the head.  Activation of trigeminal nociceptors also leads to the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), causing local vasodilation and increased neurogenic inflammation, which can further sensitize trigeminal afferents and increase/prolong pain.

The role of CGRP in migraine pathogenesis has been supported by the effectiveness of triptans (5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists that decrease CGRP release) and anti-CGRP antibodies (eg, erenumab) in treating migraine headaches.

(Choice A)  Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-producing adrenal medullary tumor that causes brief (<1 hr) episodic headaches associated with sweating, palpitations, and hypertension (rather than an aura).

(Choice B)  Amplification of epidermal growth factor receptors is associated with the development of astrocytoma and glioblastoma.  Headache and vomiting due to increased intracranial pressure are common, but symptoms are typically progressive and associated with other neurologic manifestations (eg, seizures, focal neurologic deficits).

(Choice C)  Orexin A and B are excitatory neuropeptides produced in the lateral hypothalamus during wakefulness that inhibit the transition to REM sleep.  Instead of episodic headaches, deficiency of these neuropeptides causes the daytime sleepiness, inappropriate bouts of REM sleep (ie, sleep attacks), and emotionally triggered transient muscle weakness (ie, cataplexy) seen in narcolepsy.

(Choice D)  Dysfunction of thalamocortical fiber calcium channels can contribute to the development of absence seizures, which are generalized seizures that manifest as brief (10-20 sec) staring episodes with impairment of consciousness, not recurrent headaches.

Educational objective:The pathogenesis of migraines involves a genetic predisposition to increased cerebral excitability (with subsequent cortical spreading depression), which leads to abnormal activation of meningeal trigeminal afferents and the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide, a vasoactive neuropeptide involved in the transmission of pain signals.​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌
